title: The broken gong (133–136)
hook: speak no harsh words; be silent as a broken gong and you have reached peace

segments.voice: Yesterday, all tremble: every creature flinches at the rod. Your line: all fear the rod.

Somebody in the group chat says something sharp. Thumbs start moving before the mind has caught up. The reply gets typed, and it's good. Clever. It lands. Then a reply to the reply, someone else joins in, and forty messages later nobody remembers what the first one said. Every sharp word got an answer, and every answer got an answer. It's like hitting a bell: strike it, and it rings back at you. Today's verse offers a different kind of bell, one that doesn't ring back at all.
screen: `THE SHARP MESSAGE.` → `FORTY REPLIES LATER.` → `A BELL THAT RINGS BACK.`

segments.voice: Verse one thirty-three could have been written about that group chat. In Max Müller's words: "Do not speak harshly to anybody; those who are spoken to will answer thee in the same way. Angry speech is painful, blows for blows will touch thee." Harsh words come back. That's not a threat; it's an observation anyone can check. Then the image. Verse one thirty-four: "If, like a shattered metal plate (gong), thou utter not, then thou hast reached Nirvana; contention is not known to thee." Müller added the word gong in brackets. The Pali word, kaṃsa, names bronze, a bronze vessel or plate, the kind that rings when struck. A whole gong answers every blow. A cracked one doesn't: a dull thud, then nothing. No echo, no second round. This isn't the silence of sulking, which rings for days on the inside. It isn't swallowing everything forever. It's the quiet of something that no longer needs to answer back, and the verse is bold about it: such quiet is already nirvana, and quarrel doesn't know where to find you. Then the chapter turns sober. Verse one thirty-five: "As a cowherd with his staff drives his cows into the stable, so do Age and Death drive the life of men." Life is short, and the cowherd is already walking. One more reason not to spend it on the fortieth reply.
screen: `HARSH WORDS COME BACK.` · `KAṂSA — A BRONZE GONG.` · `A CRACKED GONG DOESN'T RING BACK.` · `THE COWHERD IS ALREADY WALKING.` · then, large: `SILENT AS A BROKEN GONG.`

segments.voice: Remember a recent moment when someone's words stung and you answered back, and replay only the first line, theirs. This time, picture yourself as the cracked gong: the words arrive and land, and nothing rings, while you watch the urge to answer rise in your chest or jaw like a wave coming in and going out. You don't have to agree with them; you just don't ring.
Kamsa. Bronze: the broken gong of verse one thirty-four, cracked so it no longer rings, like one who doesn't answer back and so finds peace.
Your line: silent as a broken gong. No echo, and no second round. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Right speech, one of the steps of the eightfold path, includes refraining from harsh words, and Buddhist teachers often use the broken gong as an image for letting provocation land without answering in kind.

original.note: Pali: bronze, a bronze plate or gong, the kind that rings when struck.

trapdoor: what you thought: stay quiet and keep the peace.
what it means: be like a cracked gong: provocation lands, and nothing rings back, so the quarrel ends with you.
what a scholar hears: kaṃsa is bronze or a bronze vessel; Müller's '(gong)' is his bracketed gloss, and the verse says such quiet is already nibbāna, with no contention.
